result.summary: Pausanias continues listing Olympic victor statues. He tells how Glaucus of Carystus, a farmer's son, became a champion boxer, then notes the armed-race victors of Heraea, the Argive sculptors, and the chariot of Cleosthenes of Epidamnus, the first horse-owner to set up his statue at Olympia.

scenes.title: Glaucus the ploughman boxer
scenes.summary: Glaucus, who mended a plough with his bare hand, is sent to Olympia by his father and wins after being urged to remember the ploughshare. His statue shows him boxing.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus risks defeat and fainting from punishment in his last bout at Olympia.

scenes.title: Statues of Heraea and others
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statues of Damaretus and his family, the Argive sculptors' inscription, Iccus, and Pantarces.

scenes.title: Chariot of Cleosthenes
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the chariot of Cleosthenes of Epidamnus, the first horse-breeder to set up his statue, then Epidamnus and further boy victors.

notable_quotes.reason: Father's famous cry reminding Glaucus of his strength turned the boxing match.

analysis.text: The passage shows how athletic fame came from humble origins and is preserved through statues and inscriptions.
The statues record the Greek habit of honoring victors and show the early armed race, later abandoned.

fun_facts.text: The armed race (hoplitodromos) was introduced at Olympia in 520 BC, the 65th Olympiad.

language_notes.text: A ploughshare is the cutting blade of a plough. The point is that he used his bare hand as a hammer, which shows extraordinary strength.
The father's cry reminds Glaucus of his hand's feat on the farm, urging him to strike with the same force.
"The noble Science" is an old term for boxing as a skilled art.
The race in heavy armour (hoplite race) was run by men carrying shield, helmet and greaves. The 65th Olympiad is about 520 BC.
The pentathlum (pentathlon) was a five-event contest: running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.
The Zeus behind it was dedicated from the spoils of the Greek victory over the Persians at Platæa in 479 BC.
An elegiac couplet is a two-line verse form, a hexameter followed by a pentameter, common in inscriptions.
Epidamnus, on the Adriatic coast, was later called Dyrrhachium; Pausanias says the name came from its founder.

context_notes.text: Carystus is a city on Euboea. Glaucus the sea god was a fisherman turned deity in Greek legend, which gives the athlete a divine ancestor.
The Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian games were the other great Panhellenic festivals, so these wins make Glaucus a major champion.
Phidias was the famous sculptor who made the great Zeus at Olympia.
Offerings at Olympia could be a chariot alone, without the dedicator's statue, as with Euagoras.

literary_notes.text: The father's brief, direct cry turns a legend into a dramatic reversal, explaining the victory through the earlier ploughshare feat.
The quoted inscription gives the sculptors' own voice, serving as evidence and adding documentary authority to the narrative.
Pausanias speaks as a careful antiquarian, ranking Cleosthenes as a first and noting what he knows from what he does not.
